planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into humus-rich soil beneath trees or shrubs; this species roots wherever its trailing stems touch soil, so new plants establish quickly from layered sections.

directions: Native to woodland understories in western China, this low, evergreen, mat-forming bramble is grown mainly as a tough groundcover for dry or dappled shade under trees, where it roots at every node to knit together a dense, weed-suppressing carpet. Small white flowers in late spring give way to red, raspberry-like drupelets that are edible fresh but mild and somewhat seedy, making them more a curiosity snack for gardeners and wildlife than a serious crop. Stems are covered in soft reddish bristles rather than hooked thorns, so it is far easier to handle than typical brambles, though its vigorous spread means it needs a contained bed or a hard edge to stay in bounds. Cut back hard every few years to renew growth and prevent the mat from building up excessive old, woody stems.

planting.note: Plant divisions or bare-root stock in spring into cool, consistently moist soil in a shaded woodland or streambank setting; established plants spread slowly via low, sprawling branches.

directions: A low, sprawling, thornless currant native to cool, moist forests and streambanks across boreal Canada and the northern Appalachians, Skunk Currant is among the most shade-tolerant of all Ribes species, thriving even in fairly dense conifer shade where few other fruiting shrubs persist. The small red berries are covered in gland-tipped bristles and, like the foliage, release a distinctly skunky odor when bruised or crushed, which limits their appeal for fresh eating but does not prevent their use cooked into jam or jelly. Give it consistently damp, humus-rich soil and cool root conditions, as it struggles in heat or dry sites. It spreads gradually by low, rooting branches rather than aggressively, making it a manageable native choice for a shaded, moist woodland edge.
sources: Flora of North America — Ribes glandulosum

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into cool, acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), humus-rich soil in a shaded or high-elevation site; like other Vaccinium, it resents heat and dry, alkaline conditions.

directions: Found naturally in the deep, cool shade of high-elevation spruce-fir and northern hardwood forests along the Appalachian spine, this deciduous shrub tolerates more shade than most fruiting blueberry relatives, making it a good candidate for cool, acidic woodland gardens at higher elevations or in northern climates. Its bright red, tart, cranberry-like berries ripen in late summer and are traditionally used in jellies and sauces rather than eaten out of hand. As with other Vaccinium species, it needs consistently moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil and struggles in hot, humid lowland gardens outside its cool native range. Plant nursery-propagated stock, since seed germination is slow and erratic without extended cold stratification.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
Weakley, A.S. — Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into acidic, moist, sandy soil beneath open pine canopy; it colonizes slowly by underground rhizomes once established.

directions: Native to the pine flatwoods and sandy, moist savannas of the southeastern Coastal Plain, this low, colony-forming shrub takes its common name from the fine, soft hairs covering its young twigs and the undersides of its leaves. It tolerates the dappled, partial shade found beneath open longleaf pine canopy far better than open-sun blueberry species, making it a useful native groundcover for acidic, humid Southeastern gardens. Small black berries ripen in summer and are sweet and edible, though lightly borne compared to cultivated blueberries, and are best gathered for fresh snacking or preserves rather than large-scale harvest. Keep soil consistently moist and acidic (pH 4.5-5.5) and avoid disturbing the shallow, spreading rhizome mat once the colony is established.
sources: Weakley, A.S. — Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in fall into well-drained, humus-rich soil at the edge of tree cover; established plants tolerate summer drought better than most currants once rooted.

directions: Native to coniferous forest understories across the interior Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, this deciduous currant gets its common name from the sticky, gland-covered hairs coating its leaves and stems, which release a resinous fragrance when touched. Its cream to pale pink, tubular flowers are notably fragrant and attract early-season pollinators, and the resulting black berries are edible, if somewhat dry and seedy, and were historically eaten fresh or dried by Indigenous peoples of the region. It adapts well to the partial shade of a mixed conifer-hardwood planting and, once established, handles the dry summers typical of its native montane range better than many currants bred for garden fruit production. Prune out a portion of the oldest stems each winter to keep the shrub open and productive.
sources: Native Plant Network — Ribes viscosissimum propagation protocol
